The Case for a New Constitutional Convention

The United States should convene a new constitutional convention under Article V—not to make another narrow adjustment to an aging framework, but to confront the possibility that the framework itself no longer serves a modern democratic republic. The Constitution remains an extraordinary historical achievement, but reverence for its origins cannot substitute for honest judgment about its present performance. A governing system designed for a small, agrarian country of four million people in the eighteenth century now governs a continental, technologically advanced, deeply diverse nation of more than 330 million. Its institutional failures are no longer occasional defects. They are structural, recurring, and increasingly dangerous.

America does not merely suffer from partisan polarization, legislative gridlock, unequal representation, campaign-finance distortions, and declining public trust. It suffers from a Constitution that often turns those problems into permanent features of government. The country needs more than piecemeal amendments. It needs a serious national reconsideration of how democratic power should be organized, constrained, and made accountable.

Article V provides a lawful mechanism for precisely this moment. If two-thirds of state legislatures call for a convention, Congress must convene one for proposing amendments; any proposed changes would still require ratification by three-fourths of the states. The process is deliberately difficult, but difficulty is not impossibility. The Constitution was never meant to be a sacred artifact beyond revision. It was meant to be a framework created by the people and, when necessary, remade by the people.

A Constitution Built for Another Country

The central weakness of the current Constitution is not that it is old. Old institutions can still be effective. The problem is that it was built for political, social, and economic conditions that no longer exist.

The framers governed a population spread across thirteen states, most of whose residents lived in rural communities and whose economy was based largely on agriculture, trade, and enslaved labor. There were no political parties in the modern sense, no national media systems, no multinational corporations, no instantaneous communication, no cyberwarfare, no administrative state, no mass democracy, and no realistic expectation that citizens would directly participate in national policy debates at scale.

Today, Americans live in a nation dominated by metropolitan regions, global markets, digital platforms, complex financial systems, industrialized political communication, and immense concentrations of wealth. Yet the constitutional architecture still assumes that political power can be mediated through institutions designed to slow government, divide responsibility, and prevent national majorities from acting too quickly.

Those safeguards were understandable in 1787. In the twenty-first century, they often make democratic action nearly impossible even when problems are urgent, widely recognized, and supported by substantial majorities. Climate change, public health emergencies, economic crises, gun violence, infrastructure decay, artificial intelligence, and voting rights all demand a government capable of acting competently and legitimately. Instead, the United States repeatedly demonstrates that it can identify crises but cannot reliably respond to them.

A system that cannot govern effectively is not protected by its age. It is condemned by its results.

The Senate Is Radically Undemocratic

The clearest example is the United States Senate. Every state receives two senators regardless of population. As a result, a resident of Wyoming has vastly more influence over federal legislation than a resident of California, Texas, Florida, or New York. Small states representing a small fraction of the population can elect a majority of the Senate and block legislation favored by a decisive national majority.

This is not a minor imperfection. It means that one chamber of Congress is designed to give unequal political power to citizens based solely on where they live. The principle of “one person, one vote,” accepted in virtually every other democratic context, is abandoned in the institution that confirms judges, ratifies treaties, approves executive appointments, and can halt nearly all major legislation.

Defenders of the Senate argue that it protects federalism and prevents large states from dominating small ones. But federalism does not require permanent minority rule. States can retain meaningful authority over local governance without granting a tiny share of the national population the power to overrule everyone else. The Senate’s structure has become less a safeguard for regional diversity than a mechanism by which rural and low-population states can exercise disproportionate national control.

A new constitutional settlement should replace the Senate with a genuinely democratic second chamber, perhaps one elected proportionally, or retain a state-based chamber but ensure that representation reflects population more fairly. No modern democracy should accept extreme inequality of representation as a constitutional virtue.

The Electoral College Undermines Popular Sovereignty

The Electoral College is another relic that has outlived its justification. It allows presidential candidates to win the office while losing the national popular vote. It focuses campaigns on a handful of competitive states while rendering millions of votes in safely partisan states practically irrelevant. It turns presidential elections into contests over narrow regional coalitions rather than national mandates.

The presidency is the most powerful office in the country. Its occupant commands the military, directs the executive branch, shapes foreign policy, appoints judges, and influences the entire national agenda. There is no democratic justification for allowing the candidate preferred by fewer voters to hold that office.

The Electoral College does not preserve federalism. It distorts it. It does not encourage national unity. It encourages campaigns to ignore most of the country. It does not prevent fraud or instability. It creates incentives for litigation, recounts, and political manipulation in a small number of pivotal states.

A rewritten Constitution should establish direct national election of the president, likely through ranked-choice voting or another system that ensures majority support. A democracy should not treat the most basic question—who received the most votes—as optional.

Gridlock Has Become a System of Minority Vetoes

The Constitution divides power among branches and chambers in order to prevent tyranny. But the American system has accumulated so many veto points that it often prevents democratic governance itself.

Legislation must pass the House, the Senate, survive Senate procedural obstacles, receive presidential approval, and withstand judicial review. In practice, the Senate filibuster adds an extra supermajority requirement not found in the Constitution. A determined minority can block action even when elected majorities in both chambers and the presidency support it.

The result is a system in which it is easier to stop government than to make government work. That asymmetry rewards obstruction. Political parties gain advantage not by solving problems but by ensuring that the other side appears unable to govern. Voters grow cynical, trust collapses, and demagogues exploit the failure.

A new Constitution should preserve checks and balances while recognizing that every democratic system must be able to make decisions. It should establish clearer rules for legislation, eliminate anti-democratic supermajority practices for ordinary lawmaking, and create institutions that reward coalition-building rather than paralysis.

The choice is not between unrestrained majority rule and permanent obstruction. Functional democracies around the world demonstrate that governments can protect rights, respect regional diversity, and still act when the public demands action.

The Supreme Court Has Become an Unelected Super-Legislature

The modern Supreme Court wields extraordinary power over American life. Nine unelected justices, appointed for life, can invalidate laws passed by elected representatives, reshape voting rights, alter reproductive rights, define the scope of executive authority, and determine the meaning of broad constitutional guarantees.

Judicial review is not inherently illegitimate. Courts must protect constitutional rights and enforce legal limits. But lifetime tenure, partisan confirmation battles, and the Court’s ability to decide sweeping political questions have turned the judiciary into a central arena of ideological warfare.

The current system gives presidents who may have lost the popular vote, and senators representing a minority of Americans, the ability to shape constitutional interpretation for generations. That is not an adequate democratic foundation for a body with such immense authority.

A new constitutional convention should consider fixed terms for Supreme Court justices, such as eighteen-year staggered terms, regularized appointments, enforceable ethics rules, clearer limits on emergency rulings, and stronger mechanisms for democratic accountability. It should also reconsider the scope of judicial power in areas where courts have increasingly substituted their own policy judgments for those of elected institutions.

No democracy should rely on the hope that nine life-tenured officials will indefinitely resolve its deepest political disputes.

Money Has Captured Too Much of Politics

The framers feared monarchy and aristocracy, but they did not anticipate the modern political economy: billionaires, corporate political spending, opaque “dark money” organizations, sophisticated lobbying operations, and media ecosystems designed to monetize outrage.

In theory, every citizen has an equal voice. In practice, the wealthy have greater access, greater visibility, greater influence, and greater power to shape the political agenda. Campaigns require enormous sums of money, making candidates dependent on donors and interest groups. Lobbyists draft legislation, corporations finance political advocacy, and private wealth can purchase the attention that ordinary citizens struggle to obtain.

The legal doctrine equating political spending with speech has worsened the problem. It has made meaningful campaign-finance reform difficult even when the public broadly supports it. The result is not merely corruption in the narrow criminal sense. It is a political system structurally tilted toward those who already possess economic power.

A new Constitution should explicitly authorize robust campaign-finance regulation, require radical transparency in political spending, support public financing of elections, and protect the political equality of citizens against domination by concentrated wealth. Political liberty is meaningless if democratic institutions are effectively auctioned to the highest bidder.

Rights Need Modernization and Expansion

The Constitution’s Bill of Rights remains essential, but it is incomplete for the modern world. Americans need constitutional protections that address contemporary forms of vulnerability and power.

The right to vote should be explicit, affirmative, and enforceable—not inferred imperfectly through a patchwork of amendments and statutes. Every eligible citizen should have a guaranteed right to accessible voting, fair districting, and equal participation. Partisan gerrymandering should be constitutionally prohibited. Election administration should be independent and professional rather than vulnerable to partisan interference.

Privacy also requires a modern constitutional guarantee. The framers protected people against unreasonable searches of “persons, houses, papers, and effects,” but today personal information is stored in phones, databases, cloud services, biometric systems, and private platforms. A government—or corporation—that can track a person’s movements, communications, purchases, health information, and political activity possesses a form of power the eighteenth century could not imagine.

A renewed Constitution should also recognize that democracy depends on basic social security. This need not mean constitutionalizing every policy dispute, but it should mean acknowledging that citizens cannot meaningfully exercise political freedom when they lack access to education, health care, safe housing, clean air and water, or basic economic security. Liberty is not merely freedom from government interference; it is also the practical ability to live with dignity and participate in public life.

Amendment by Amendment Is No Longer Enough

Some will argue that the United States should simply amend the existing Constitution. But the amendment process itself reveals the depth of the problem. Requiring approval by three-fourths of the states means that a small minority of the population can prevent reforms favored by a large national majority.

Even reforms with broad public support—abolishing the Electoral College, establishing voting rights protections, reforming campaign finance, imposing judicial term limits, addressing gun violence, or creating more representative institutions—may be effectively impossible under the current rules. The system is structured to preserve itself.

Incremental reform also cannot solve interlocking constitutional failures. The Senate, Electoral College, judicial appointment process, amendment rules, partisan gerrymandering, and legislative paralysis reinforce one another. Changing one institution while leaving the rest intact may simply shift dysfunction elsewhere.

A convention offers something ordinary amendment campaigns do not: an opportunity to examine the entire structure at once. It would allow the country to ask foundational questions. How should representation work? What powers should states retain? How should national majorities govern while minority rights remain protected? What rights does citizenship require in a digital and unequal society? How should executive power be constrained? How can government act decisively without becoming authoritarian?

Those questions cannot be avoided forever. The only question is whether Americans will confront them through a lawful democratic process or wait until institutional failure makes a crisis unavoidable.

Fear of a Convention Is Not a Reason to Avoid One

The strongest objection to a new convention is fear: fear of a “runaway convention,” fear that extremists would dominate it, fear that established rights could be endangered, fear that the process would deepen division rather than resolve it.

Those fears are real, and they deserve serious attention. But they are not an argument for constitutional complacency. The current system already endangers rights, democratic accountability, and public stability. Refusing to reform a failing system because reform carries risks is not prudence. It is surrender to decline.

Moreover, Article V includes a crucial safeguard: ratification by three-fourths of the states. No proposed constitutional transformation would become law merely because convention delegates endorsed it. It would require broad, sustained national support across regions and political cultures. That is a demanding standard, but democratic legitimacy should be demanding when the nation’s fundamental charter is at stake.

A convention could also be designed with strong procedural protections: transparent delegate selection, public deliberation, bipartisan or nonpartisan commissions, disclosure rules, expert testimony, citizen assemblies, and clear ratification procedures. The goal should not be to hand the country over to ideological factions. It should be to create the most inclusive, deliberative, and democratic constitutional process in American history.

The 1787 convention itself exceeded its original mandate under the Articles of Confederation, yet it produced a new governing charter because the old system had plainly failed. Today’s Americans should not imitate the founders blindly. But they should imitate their willingness to recognize when inherited institutions no longer meet national needs.

A New Constitution Should Build a Functional Democracy

A modern constitutional convention should aim not merely to repair isolated defects but to create a government that is democratic, competent, rights-protecting, and trusted. Among the reforms it should consider are:

  • Direct popular election of the president, potentially using ranked-choice voting.
  • A restructured legislature with more equal representation and fewer opportunities for minority veto.
  • Independent redistricting commissions and constitutional protection against gerrymandering.
  • Explicit, enforceable voting rights for all citizens.
  • Fixed terms and enforceable ethics standards for Supreme Court justices.
  • Clear limits on executive emergency powers and stronger congressional oversight.
  • Public financing of elections, transparency requirements, and authority to regulate political spending.
  • Modern digital privacy rights and protections against mass surveillance.
  • A more realistic amendment procedure that permits democratic reform without making every change nearly impossible.
  • Stronger protections for civil rights, reproductive autonomy, environmental security, and equal citizenship.

Not every proposal must be adopted, and reasonable people will disagree about details. But the conversation must begin from the recognition that the present system is not functioning as its defenders claim. It is producing repeated democratic failures: leaders elected without national majorities, legislatures unable to legislate, courts acting as political institutions, and citizens who increasingly believe their government does not represent them.

The greatest danger is not that Americans might revise their Constitution. The greatest danger is that they will continue treating it as beyond revision while its institutions lose legitimacy and effectiveness.

The Constitution should be respected because it has helped sustain American self-government. But respect is not worship. A constitutional order earns loyalty by serving the people who live under it. When it ceases to provide equal representation, effective government, meaningful accountability, and secure rights, citizens have both the authority and the responsibility to demand change.

A new constitutional convention would be difficult, contentious, and uncertain. So was the founding itself. But democratic self-government has never been easy, and no generation is entitled to let institutional decay become the inheritance of the next.

The United States needs the courage to admit that its constitutional crisis is not merely a crisis of politicians, parties, or personalities. It is a crisis of structure. The country’s governing machinery is failing because it was designed for a different age and has been stretched beyond its capacity. Article V exists because the framers knew that no constitution, including their own, could foresee every future.

The time has come to use it.

High ratification threshold as protection

The case for replacing rather than merely amending the Constitution

A smaller but more sweeping group believes the accumulated problems are too interconnected for isolated amendments. They may argue that the country needs a comprehensive rewrite to address:

The United States Constitution, the world’s oldest written national charter, was designed to be enduring—a flexible framework capable of adapting to the needs of a dynamic nation. I. The Constitution Has Been Subverted, Not Evolved

The Founders intended the Constitution to be amended through a deliberate, consensus-driven process—one that required either congressional approval (Article V, Section 3) or state conventions (Article V, Section 2). Yet for over two centuries, the system has been gutted by partisan gridlock and judicial overreach. Wade, Dobbs, Citizens United). The 17th Amendment (1913), which abolished the election of senators by state legislatures, was supposed to make the Senate more democratic—but it instead turned it into a partisan battleground where small states and rural interests dominate disproportionately. The Electoral College, once a compromise, now ensures that minority rule is institutionalized—a president can win without a popular majority (as in 2000 and 2016). The Senate filibuster allows a minority of 41 senators to block any legislation, rendering the government permanently dysfunctional. And the Supreme Court’s lifetime appointments mean that ideological extremists (like Clarence Thomas, Samuel Alito, and Amy Coney Barrett) sit for decades, imposing their vision on the nation.

This is not evolution—it is constitutional decay.

The Founders feared tyranny of the majority—the idea that unchecked democracy could lead to mob rule. America’s Constitution is a brilliant artifact of its era—and a failing operating system for ours. We run a 21st‑century superpower on 18th‑century architecture patched by sporadic updates, and then wonder why basic governance falters, why national majorities lose to entrenched minorities, and why urgent problems linger for decades. The country needs a peaceful, transparent, and democratic refounding. An Article V convention—called by the states and culminating in ratification by the people—offers the only viable path to radically restructure or even replace the Constitution so that American self‑government can work again.

The case for a new convention begins with first principles: a constitution is not scripture; it is a tool. Tools are judged by performance—do they deliver legitimacy, representation, governability, and adaptability? On each count, our current design is failing.

Representation. The Senate’s entrenched malapportionment gives small populations outsized power. California and Wyoming have the same number of senators despite a population gap of roughly 68 to 1. By 2040, about 70% of Americans will likely be represented by just 30 senators while 30% will control 70. This isn’t a minor quirk; it warps the legislative process, judicial appointments, and national priorities. The Electoral College further compounds the problem: in two of the last six presidential elections, the popular‑vote winner lost, and future campaigns increasingly target a shrinking set of swing states rather than the nation. House representation is distorted by single‑member districts and extreme gerrymandering. Altogether, a voter’s political weight is determined less by citizenship than by their state boundary lines.

Governability. The Constitution disperses power across so many veto points that even popular, urgent reforms routinely die. Fixed presidential terms make it hard to resolve crises of confidence; the debt ceiling invites hostage‑taking; shutdowns recur; and divided government often means paralyzed government. Presidentialism without a realistic no‑confidence mechanism produces prolonged stalemate. Meanwhile, Congress delegates swathes of lawmaking to agencies and then sues those agencies for acting—an unstable workaround for a legislative body designed for stalemate in a century that requires speed.

Adaptability. Article V’s amendment process—requiring supermajorities in Congress and three‑fourths of the states—was meant to ensure stability. It now ensures sclerosis. Only two amendments have been added in more than half a century, one of which originated in 1789. The very features that need revising—Senate malapportionment and the Electoral College—are protected by small‑state veto. A system that cannot correct its own known defects will grow brittle, delegitimize itself, and invite extraconstitutional workarounds.

Judicial overconcentration. Lifetime tenure, sporadic vacancies, and polarized confirmations have turned the Supreme Court into a high‑stakes, low‑accountability super‑legislature. A small, ideologically coherent majority can reshape national policy for a generation, even when durable popular majorities disagree. This is not a critique of any one decision; it is a structural critique of how much is decided by how few, for how long, with how little democratic feedback.

A rights architecture out of step with modern governance. The Constitution brilliantly protects many negative liberties but is thin on affirmative guarantees essential to a modern democracy: the right to vote as a positive, enforceable right with national standards; equal representation; data privacy; clean air and water; a baseline of health care or education. These are not partisan wish lists; they are the basic prerequisites of civic equality and effective citizenship in a complex society.

Some argue we should pursue incremental reforms. But the most consequential fixes are locked behind the very gates that need changing. You cannot meaningfully address the Senate’s distortion or the Electoral College through ordinary legislation. You cannot reliably curb gerrymandering or set national voting standards without inviting judicial vetoes from a court appointed through unrepresentative mechanisms. We are in a constitutional cul‑de‑sac; turning around requires a new road.

An Article V convention is the constitutional way to build that road. Two‑thirds of state legislatures can call a convention to propose amendments, and any proposals still require ratification by three‑fourths of the states. The process is both bold and safe: bold because it lets Americans revisit fundamentals; safe because nothing becomes law without extensive, public ratification. Fears of a “runaway” convention misunderstand the finality of ratification: if the public does not want a change, it will not happen.

What should a new constitutional settlement include? Reasonable people will differ, but a reform agenda that restores legitimacy, governability, and rights might include:

  • Democratic representation

    • Replace or neutralize the Electoral College with a national popular vote, using ranked‑choice ballots to ensure majority support.
    • Transform the Senate into a chamber of regions with limited, clearly defined powers—or abolish it in favor of a proportional, unicameral legislature—so national policy reflects national majorities.

The Case for a New Constitutional Convention: Reclaiming Democracy from a Broken System

The United States faces a litany of systemic issues that the current Constitution either fails to address or actively exacerbates. First, the structure of our government, particularly the bicameral legislature and the Electoral College, perpetuates gross inequities in representation. Third, the Constitution fails to adequately safeguard against the concentration of power and the erosion of democratic norms. The vague language around executive authority, combined with historical precedents like the expansion of presidential war powers, has allowed the executive branch to amass unchecked influence. Article V provides a rarely used but critical mechanism for profound change: a Constitutional Convention called by two-thirds of state legislatures. Another concern is that a convention could deepen division in an already polarized nation. The original Constitutional Convention of 1787 was itself a contentious process, marked by deep disagreements over slavery and representation, yet it produced a framework that, while imperfect, laid the foundation for progress. Convening a new Constitutional Convention under Article V is not a radical act of destruction but a courageous act of renewal, a chance to reclaim the democratic ideals that inspired the nation’s founding while addressing the realities of today.

Incremental reform has proven impossible—Congress, the Supreme Court, and state legislatures are all incentivized to preserve the broken system that elevates their authority. The only viable path to restore democratic accountability, address systemic inequity, and adapt to 21st-century challenges is to convene a safeguarded Article V Constitutional Convention: a people-led process to radically restructure or rewrite the Constitution, with ironclad safeguards to prevent a “runaway” body from eroding core civil liberties.

The Constitution’s foundational flaws are not quirks of interpretation; they are intentional 18th-century compromises that have festered into existential threats to democracy. The Senate’s malapportionment, a concession to slaveholding states that feared being outvoted by more populous northern states, now gives rural, conservative voters 18 times more political power than urban, diverse voters. This imbalance has blocked action on climate change (supported by 73% of Americans), gun control (supported by 60%), and universal healthcare (supported by 58%)—policies that majority rule would demand but that the Senate’s lopsided representation strangles. The Electoral College, another slaveholder compromise (designed to inflate the political power of states with enslaved populations via the three-fifths clause), has now allowed five presidents to take office without winning the popular vote, undermining the basic principle of “one person, one vote.” Lifetime Supreme Court appointments, a provision crafted when the average life expectancy was 38 (compared to 79 today), have turned judicial nominations into partisan bloodbaths, giving unelected judges the power to override popular policy for decades. Even the Constitution’s amendment process—requiring 34 states to call a convention and 38 to ratify changes—was designed to be nearly insurmountable: in 236 years, only 27 amendments have been adopted, most of them minor (e.g., banning alcohol and then unbanning it) or correcting post-Civil War injustices that the original framers deliberately ignored.

Incremental reform has hit a brick wall because the institutions tasked with fixing the system are the ones that benefit from its flaws. Congress has no incentive to ban gerrymandering: incumbents rely on partisan districting to win 90% of reelection bids. The Supreme Court has ruled that partisan gerrymandering is a “political question” beyond its purview, abandoning its role as a check on democratic erosion. State legislatures, many of which are gerrymandered themselves, have blocked ballot initiatives to reform the Electoral College (e.g., the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact, which has stalled in swing states). Even grassroots campaigns to pressure lawmakers have failed: lobbying groups spend $3.7 billion annually to protect the status quo, and incumbents face little risk of defeat from challengers who lack access to that funding. The conclusion is unavoidable: the system is self-perpetuating. To break it, we need a process independent of the institutions that have broken it.

Critics warn of a “runaway convention”—a body of unaccountable delegates that could erase the First Amendment, roll back civil rights, or install a authoritarian regime. This fear is not unfounded: the 1787 convention was a runaway body itself, discarding its mandate to revise the Articles of Confederation and writing a new constitution in secret. But this risk can be mitigated with ironclad safeguards designed to make the convention the most inclusive, transparent democratic process in U.S. history. First, delegate selection must be tied to population equity: each state’s delegation would be proportional to its population, not its senatorial representation, and delegates would be elected via ranked-choice voting to ensure marginalized groups (Black, Indigenous, Latinx, disabled, and low-income Americans) are represented. Second, all deliberations would be broadcast live, with no closed-door sessions, and all draft proposals would be posted online for public comment 30 days before a vote. To understand the benefits, one must understand the hurdle. Under Article V:

The Case for a New Constitutional Convention: Why America Must Rebuild Its Foundation

Introduction

The United States Constitution, ratified in 1789, stands as one of history's most remarkable political documents. It was also, by its framers' own admission, a product of compromise, improvisation, and educated guesswork. Over two centuries later, that document—amended only twenty-seven times, with ten of those amendments arriving in a single package—now governs a nation of 330 million people, a $27 trillion economy, and a global military superpower that its authors could not have conceived in their most extravagant imaginations. The question is not whether the framers were brilliant; they were. The question is whether a document designed for thirteen agrarian coastal states with a total population smaller than modern-day Houston can continue to serve as the operating system for the most complex republic in human history. The honest answer, increasingly evident across every dimension of American governance, is that it cannot—at least not without radical structural revision. It is time to invoke the Convention mechanism provided by Article V of the Constitution itself and undertake the serious, generation-defining work of rebuilding America's constitutional architecture.

This is not a radical position. It is, in fact, the position the framers themselves anticipated. Article V explicitly provides two paths for amendment: proposal by two-thirds of Congress, or proposal by a convention called upon application by two-thirds of state legislatures. The framers included the convention mechanism precisely because they understood that Congress might one day become too self-interested, too paralyzed, or too captured to reform itself. That day has arrived. The convention path is not a loophole or an emergency measure—it is a feature, deliberately engineered by men who understood that constitutions must evolve or die.

I. The Democratic Deficit: A Government That Cannot Represent Its People

The most fundamental problem with the current constitutional order is that it has produced a system of representation so distorted that it can no longer plausibly claim to reflect the will of the governed.

The Senate remains the most malapportioned legislative body in any major democracy on Earth. Wyoming's 576,000 residents receive the same representation as California's 39 million. This is not a minor statistical curiosity—it is a structural feature that gives roughly 18% of the American population the power to command a Senate majority. The Senate confirms Supreme Court justices, ratifies treaties, and can block all legislation. The result is that a determined minority, drawn from the least populous states, can exercise an effective veto over the preferences of enormous supermajorities of the American public. The standard defense—that the Senate was designed to represent states as sovereign entities—presupposes a theory of state sovereignty that the Civil War, the Fourteenth Amendment, and two centuries of federal supremacy have rendered largely fictional.

The Electoral College has now produced two presidents in the twenty-first century alone who lost the popular vote. Whatever justification this institution may have had in an era of limited communication, widespread illiteracy, and genuine concern about mob rule, it now functions primarily as a mechanism for concentrating presidential campaigns in a handful of swing states while rendering the votes of tens of millions of Americans in non-competitive states functionally irrelevant. It distorts policy, warps campaign strategy, and periodically installs leaders who lack majoritarian support—an outcome that would be considered a democratic crisis in any other developed nation.

The House of Representatives, while nominally proportional, is capped at 435 members by a statute from 1929, meaning each representative now serves roughly 760,000 constituents—a ratio so large that meaningful constituent-representative relationships are nearly impossible and that virtually guarantees dominance by organized interest groups and professional political operatives over ordinary citizens.

These are not bugs that can be fixed with clever statutory reforms. They are hardwired into the constitutional text and protected by an amendment process so demanding that structural reform through the traditional congressional route is essentially impossible—particularly since the very actors who would need to propose such amendments are the primary beneficiaries of the existing distortions.

II. Institutional Paralysis: A System Designed for Gridlock in an Era Requiring Action

The Constitution's system of separated powers and checks and balances was designed to prevent tyranny. It has succeeded—but at the cost of creating a government increasingly incapable of effective action on virtually any major issue.

The framers designed a system premised on the assumption that faction could be managed through institutional competition. What they did not anticipate—and could not have anticipated—was the emergence of disciplined, ideologically sorted national political parties that would transform separated institutions into warring camps. When the president, House, and Senate are controlled by different parties (an increasingly common occurrence), the system does not produce the creative compromise the framers envisioned. It produces paralysis, government shutdowns, governance by executive order, and legislative reliance on omnibus bills and reconciliation procedures that make a mockery of deliberative democracy.

Consider the policy landscape: the United States cannot pass comprehensive immigration reform despite decades of bipartisan public support. It cannot rationalize its tax code. It cannot address infrastructure decay at the pace required. It cannot enact coherent climate policy despite overwhelming scientific consensus. It cannot reform its healthcare system despite spending nearly twice what comparable nations spend for worse aggregate outcomes. It cannot even reliably pass a federal budget through regular order. These are not failures of political will alone—they are the predictable consequences of a constitutional structure that multiplies veto points to such a degree that organized opposition to any change will almost always defeat organized support for it.

The framers' Constitution was designed for an era when the default condition of government inaction was relatively benign—when the nascent republic faced few problems that required rapid, coordinated federal response. In the twenty-first century, government paralysis is not benign. Climate change, pandemic preparedness, artificial intelligence governance, and economic globalization all demand a state capable of acting decisively and adaptively. The current constitutional structure is fundamentally hostile to such capacity.

III. The Judiciary as Superlegislature: An Unintended Constitutional Monarchy

Perhaps no feature of the current system would astonish the framers more than the role the Supreme Court has assumed. Through the power of judicial review—itself not explicitly enumerated in the Constitution but asserted by the Court in Marbury v. Madison—nine unelected lawyers with lifetime tenure now serve as the ultimate arbiters of virtually every significant policy question in American life.

The Court determines the scope of reproductive rights, the meaning of the Second Amendment, the limits of executive power, the boundaries of federal regulatory authority, the rules of campaign finance, and the legality of affirmative action. Justices appointed by presidents who lost the popular vote, confirmed by senators representing a minority of the population, now exercise functionally unreviewable power over the most intimate and consequential aspects of American life—and they do so for decades, frequently long after the political coalitions that produced them have dissolved.

The lifetime appointment of federal judges was defensible in an era when life expectancy was far shorter and when the Court's role was far more circumscribed. Today, a justice appointed at fifty may serve for thirty-five or forty years, shaping law for generations based on a single confirmation vote. This is not judicial independence—it is judicial oligarchy, and it has increasingly made Supreme Court appointments the central dramatic event of American politics, distorting every other institution in the process.

No other major democracy grants its constitutional court this combination of power, tenure, and insulation from democratic accountability. Term limits, mandatory retirement ages, altered appointment processes, or a restructured court could address these problems—but all would likely require constitutional amendment, and the current amendment process makes such reforms effectively unachievable.

IV. The Amendment Process Itself: A Lock Without a Key

This brings us to the deepest structural problem of all. Article V requires either two-thirds of both houses of Congress or two-thirds of state legislatures to propose amendments, and three-fourths of state legislatures or state conventions to ratify them. This means that thirteen states—potentially representing less than 4% of the national population—can block any constitutional amendment.

This supermajority requirement was defensible when it was adopted. It has become a straitjacket. The Constitution has not been meaningfully amended in structural terms since the 1960s and early 1970s (the Twenty-Sixth Amendment, ratifying the eighteen-year-old vote, was ratified in 1971). The Equal Rights Amendment, despite commanding broad popular support, could not clear the ratification threshold. Proposals for Electoral College reform, campaign finance reform, Senate reapportionment, and dozens of other structural changes have repeatedly died not because they lacked majority support—many have commanded supermajority support in public opinion—but because the ratification process gives a tiny minority of the population an absolute veto.

A constitutional system that cannot be updated through its own internal mechanisms is not stable—it is brittle. And brittle systems do not bend; they break. The convention mechanism offers a path to comprehensive reform that does not depend on the cooperation of a Congress that has every institutional incentive to resist change.

V. The Anachronism Problem: Provisions That No Longer Serve Any Defensible Purpose

Beyond the structural issues of representation and institutional design, the Constitution contains numerous provisions that are simply artifacts of eighteenth-century compromises that no longer bear any rational relationship to contemporary governance.

The Third Amendment's prohibition on quartering soldiers is a historical relic. The Second Amendment's prefatory militia clause generates endless interpretive disputes that its authors could never have anticipated in an era of semiautomatic weapons and standing armies. The concept of sovereign immunity, the structure of federalism, the allocation of war powers—all of these reflect compromises and assumptions rooted in a world that no longer exists.

More fundamentally, the Constitution is silent on issues that now define the basic social contract in every other advanced democracy: healthcare, education, housing, environmental protection, digital privacy, and the rights of workers. The framers could not have addressed these issues because they did not exist in their recognizable modern form. But the result is a constitutional order that provides elaborate protections for eighteenth-century concerns while offering no foundational guidance on the central challenges of twenty-first-century life.

A convention would allow the nation to draft a document that addresses the world as it actually is, rather than forcing every contemporary problem through the interpretive machinery of a document written before the invention of the steam engine.

VI. Comparative Evidence: Other Democracies Rewrite Their Constitutions

The American reverence for its Constitution is unique among democracies—and not in an entirely healthy way. The political scientist Zachary Elkins and his colleagues have documented that the average national constitution lasts approximately seventeen years. This is not because other nations are less serious about constitutional governance; it is because they understand that constitutions are tools, not sacred texts, and that tools must be updated to remain useful.

Germany rewrote its constitution after World War II and has amended it dozens of times since. France is on its Fifth Republic. South Africa drafted one of the world's most admired constitutions in 1996. These nations did not abandon constitutionalism by rewriting their foundational documents—they strengthened it, adapting their governance structures to the demands of their times.

The United States, by contrast, has treated its Constitution with a reverence more appropriate to religious scripture than to a governing document. This constitutional veneration—what the legal scholar Sanford Levinson has called "constitutional faith"—has become an obstacle to the very self-governance the document was meant to enable.

VII. Addressing the Objections

Critics of a convention raise several objections, all of which deserve serious engagement.

"A runaway convention could destroy existing rights." This concern is understandable but overstated. Any proposals emerging from a convention would still require ratification by three-fourths of the states, providing a substantial check against radical or destructive proposals. Moreover, the current system is already eroding rights through judicial reinterpretation, executive overreach, and legislative paralysis—the status quo is not a safe harbor.

"The current political environment is too polarized for a convention." This objection gets the causation backward. The political environment is polarized in significant part because the constitutional structure creates incentives for polarization, rewards obstruction, and prevents the majoritarian resolution of contested issues. A well-structured convention, with carefully designed rules of procedure and broad representation, could become an instrument for rebuilding civic trust precisely because it would operate outside the poisoned channels of ordinary congressional politics.

"The framers' Constitution has served us well for over two centuries." It has—but survival is not the same as success, and past performance does not guarantee future results. The Constitution also presided over slavery, the disenfranchisement of women, Jim Crow, Japanese internment, and innumerable other moral catastrophes. That the republic has endured is a testament to the resilience of the American people, not necessarily to the perfection of their governing document.

"We should pursue incremental reform rather than wholesale revision." Incremental reform through the existing amendment process has been tried for generations and has failed. The system is designed to resist change, and it does so with remarkable efficiency. At some point, the insistence on incrementalism becomes not prudence but paralysis by another name.

VIII. What a Convention Could Achieve

A convention would have the opportunity to address the full sweep of structural dysfunction:

  • Redesigning the legislature to ensure proportional representation, eliminate or reform the Senate's malapportionment, and restore the House to a size that permits meaningful representation.
  • Reforming the executive to clarify war powers, constrain emergency authorities, and establish clearer lines of accountability.
  • Restructuring the judiciary to impose term limits, alter the appointment process, and clarify the scope of judicial review.
  • Modernizing rights protections to address privacy, digital surveillance, environmental sustainability, education, and healthcare.
  • Reforming the amendment process itself to make future constitutional evolution possible without requiring the kind of extraordinary mobilization that a convention represents.
  • Addressing electoral democracy by establishing national standards for voting rights, eliminating or reforming the Electoral College, and constraining partisan gerrymandering at the constitutional level.

These are not utopian fantasies. They are features of constitutional systems in dozens of functioning democracies around the world. The United States is not incapable of achieving them—it has simply trapped itself in a constitutional structure that makes achieving them nearly impossible through ordinary means.

Conclusion

The framers of the Constitution were, above all, pragmatists. They gathered in Philadelphia in 1787 not to venerate the Articles of Confederation but to replace them, because the existing system was not working. They understood that political institutions must serve the living, not bind them to the preferences of the dead. They included the convention mechanism in Article V because they knew that future generations would face challenges they could not foresee, and they trusted those generations to rise to meet them.

We are that generation. The challenges before us—democratic erosion, institutional paralysis, representational distortion, judicial supremacy, and constitutional obsolescence—are not problems that can be tweeted, litigated, or incrementally legislated away. They are structural, and they require structural solutions.

Calling a constitutional convention is not an act of disrespect toward the founders. It is the highest form of respect: it is taking seriously their belief that the people of the United States possess the wisdom and the right to govern themselves, and that no generation—however brilliant—should govern from the grave. Model Response:

Arguments for an Article V Constitutional Convention

Background

Article V provides two paths for amendments: through Congress (used for all 27 existing amendments) or through a convention called when 2/3 of state legislatures (34 states) apply. Supporters span the political spectrum, though they often want very different outcomes.

Arguments That the Current System Is Broken

Structural criticisms supporters raise:

  • The Constitution was designed for a small agrarian republic of ~4 million people and may not adequately serve a complex nation of 330+ million
  • The amendment process through Congress is effectively frozen — only one amendment has passed since 1971 — meaning known problems cannot be corrected through normal channels
  • Congress has little incentive to propose amendments that would limit its own power, creating a structural conflict of interest
  • Many provisions reflect 18th-century compromises (particularly around slavery and small-state power) whose rationales no longer apply

Democratic legitimacy concerns:

  • The Senate gives Wyoming (population ~580,000) equal representation to California (~39 million), creating a roughly 68:1 disparity in per-capita representation
  • The Electoral College can produce presidents who lose the popular vote, which has happened twice in recent memory (2000, 2016)
  • Gerrymandering, which some argue could be constitutionally addressed, distorts House representation
  • Washington D.C. residents (~700,000 people) have no voting representation in Congress
  • The amendment process itself allows 13 states representing a small fraction of the population to block any change

Proposed Reforms and Their Supposed Benefits

Governance Structure

Supporters argue a convention could:

  • Reform or replace the Electoral College to better reflect democratic will
  • Address Senate malapportionment or restructure the chamber
  • Establish clearer rules for executive power, which has expanded well beyond what the framers envisioned
  • Create more functional mechanisms for breaking legislative gridlock
  • Establish independent redistricting requirements
  • Clarify the separation of powers, which has become blurred through executive orders, agency rulemaking, and congressional delegation

Fiscal and Economic Issues

From the right, primarily:

  • Balanced budget amendment — arguably the closest active movement to reaching the 34-state threshold
  • Spending limitations or tax restrictions
  • Limiting federal regulatory power
  • Supporters argue these would impose fiscal discipline Congress has proven unable or unwilling to maintain on its own

From the left:

  • Overturning Citizens United and establishing campaign finance regulation authority
  • Addressing wealth concentration through structural reforms
  • Enshrining economic rights (healthcare, education, housing)

Rights and Protections

Supporters suggest explicitly addressing:

  • Privacy rights in the digital age — the Constitution predates any concept of electronic surveillance, data collection, or digital life
  • Environmental protections or rights of future generations
  • Clarifying the scope of the Second Amendment rather than leaving it to shifting court interpretations
  • Term limits for Supreme Court justices (and possibly Congress), addressing what some see as excessive accumulation of power in unelected, life-tenured judges
  • Voting rights protections that go beyond the current patchwork of amendments

Modernization

  • The Constitution contains no mention of administrative agencies, which now constitute the vast majority of federal governance
  • Foreign policy powers are ambiguously divided in ways that have led to undeclared wars lasting decades
  • Emergency powers lack clear constitutional boundaries
  • Supporters argue that a modernized document could provide clearer frameworks for how government actually operates today, rather than maintaining the fiction that 18th-century categories neatly apply

The "Convention of States" Movement Specifically

This is the most organized current effort, generally conservative-leaning, seeking a convention limited to:

  • Federal fiscal restraints
  • Limiting federal jurisdiction and power
  • Term limits for federal officials

Their core argument is that the federal government has far exceeded its originally intended scope and that only the states, acting collectively outside Congress, can restore the balance. They frame Article V's convention mechanism as the founders' intentional "emergency brake" for precisely this situation.

As of recent counts, they have secured roughly 19 state applications, needing 34.

Philosophical and Democratic Arguments

The "living generation" argument:

  • Jefferson himself suggested constitutions should be revisited every generation (~19 years)
  • The average national constitution worldwide lasts roughly 17 years; the U.S. Constitution is over 230 years old
  • Supporters argue that binding a modern society to an 18th-century framework — especially one that most living citizens never consented to — raises fundamental democratic legitimacy questions
  • Many other democracies (France on its Fifth Republic, for instance) have successfully replaced or overhauled their constitutions

The "known problems" argument:

  • Many constitutional scholars across the spectrum can identify provisions that are problematic, outdated, or ambiguous
  • The current system effectively makes these problems permanent
  • A convention would allow comprehensive consideration rather than the piecemeal single-amendment approach

The federalism argument:

  • A convention would empower state legislatures — closer to the people — rather than Congress
  • It would reflect the constitutional design of distributed sovereignty
  • Some supporters see it as the ultimate expression of popular self-governance

What Supporters Say to Common Objections

"It could be a runaway convention":

  • Supporters argue that any proposals still require ratification by 3/4 of states (38), making radical changes extremely unlikely unless broadly supported
  • Historical precedent (the 1787 convention did exceed its mandate, but the result required ratification)
  • Many legal scholars argue conventions can be limited in scope by the state applications

"It's too risky":

  • Supporters counter that the status quo carries its own risks — growing dysfunction, declining public trust, increasingly bitter disputes over constitutional interpretation
  • The ratification requirement serves as a safety valve
  • Not acting may be riskier than acting

"Special interests would capture it":

  • Supporters argue the current system is already captured by special interests, and a convention with state-level delegates might actually be more resistant to this
  • Transparent proceedings could be required

Honest Caveats

It's worth noting several things about these arguments:

  • Supporters on the left and right often want contradictory changes, meaning any actual convention would involve enormous conflict
  • The mechanics of a convention are largely untested and legally uncertain — there are unresolved questions about delegate selection, scope limitation, and voting procedures
  • Many constitutional scholars, both liberal and conservative, oppose a convention out of concern about unpredictability
  • Some arguments for a convention conflate problems with the Constitution itself and problems with political culture that no document can fix
  • The 3/4 ratification requirement means any outcome would need extraordinarily broad support, which some see as a safeguard and others see as making the exercise pointless

The strongest version of the pro-convention argument is essentially: the American people should have the right to deliberately choose their form of government rather than inheriting one by default, and Article V exists precisely to make that possible.

"We the People — Again"

A Speech Advocating for an Article V Constitutional Convention

Fellow Americans,

Two hundred and thirty-seven years ago, a group of delegates gathered in Philadelphia, locked the doors, drew the curtains, and did something radical — something dangerous — something absolutely essential. They looked at a failing system of government, the Articles of Confederation, and they did not tinker around the edges. They did not add a clause here or a revision there. They started over. They built something new.

But here's what too many of us have forgotten: those Founders never intended for that document to be a sacred relic, sealed under glass, untouchable for eternity. They expected us to change it. They demanded that we would. Thomas Jefferson wrote that no generation has the right to bind the next, that constitutions should be revisited every nineteen or twenty years. George Mason — George Mason — refused to sign the Constitution in part because he feared it would be too difficult to amend. I am here today to tell you that it is time. It is time to use the tool the Founders themselves placed in Article V of the Constitution. It is time to call a Convention — not to burn down what they built, but to honor their vision by doing exactly what they did: facing the failures of our system honestly and having the courage to build something better.

The System Is Broken — And Everyone Knows It

Let me ask you something. Look around this country. Look at the polls, look at the data, look at your neighbors' faces. Do you believe — does anyone genuinely believe — that our government is functioning?

Congress has an approval rating that hovers, in good times, somewhere between root canals and traffic jams. We lurch from crisis to crisis — government shutdowns, debt ceiling standoffs, filibusters that paralyze even the most modest legislation. We have a system where the will of vast majorities is routinely thwarted by procedural tricks, by gerrymandered districts, by the suffocating influence of money so deep and so pervasive that the average citizen's policy preferences have, according to researchers at Princeton and Northwestern, a near-zero statistical impact on what actually becomes law.

Near. Zero.

Let that settle in.

We do not have a government of the people. We have a government of inertia. We have a government designed for thirteen agricultural states clinging to the Atlantic seaboard, and we are asking it to govern a continental superpower of 330 million souls navigating artificial intelligence, climate disruption, global terrorism, and economic transformations that would be unrecognizable to anyone who walked the streets of Philadelphia in 1787.

And listen — this is not a partisan argument. I am not here to tell you the problem is the Left or the Right. The problem is structural. The machinery itself is grinding to a halt. You can put the finest drivers in the world behind the wheel of a car with a cracked engine block, and that car is not going to run.

We have a cracked engine block.

Article V: The Tool They Gave Us

Now, there are those who hear the words "Constitutional Convention" and recoil. They imagine chaos. They imagine a runaway body that will shred the Bill of Rights and leave us in anarchy.

I understand that fear. But I want to challenge it — directly and forcefully.

First: Article V is not a loophole. It is not a back door. It is the front door. It is right there in the text of the Constitution itself. The Founders created two paths to amendment — one through Congress, and one that bypasses Congress entirely, because they knew — they knew — that a day might come when Congress itself was the problem. When the legislature was so captured, so calcified, so consumed by its own self-preservation that it would never voluntarily reform itself.

Does that sound familiar?

Article V says that upon the application of two-thirds of the state legislatures, Congress shall call a convention for proposing amendments. Not may. Shall. It is a mandate. It is the emergency provision of our republic, placed there for exactly the kind of moment we are living through.

And second — let me address the "runaway convention" fear head-on. Any amendment proposed by a convention must still be ratified by three-fourths of the states. That is thirty-eight out of fifty. Do you understand what an extraordinary safeguard that is? You cannot get thirty-eight states to agree on anything unless it reflects a deep, broad, durable consensus of the American people. The idea that a convention would somehow secretly abolish free speech or the right to bear arms or any cherished liberty — and that thirty-eight states would then ratify that abolition — is not a serious concern. It is a fear deployed to keep us paralyzed. And I, for one, refuse to be paralyzed any longer.

What Could We Fix?

So what would we address? What would we bring to the table?

Let me offer a vision — not a final blueprint, because the beauty of a convention is that it belongs to all of us — but a vision of what's possible.

Money in politics. We could finally, definitively establish that the spending of money is not the same as the exercise of speech — that democracy means government responsive to voters, not to donors. We could write into our foundational law what eighty percent of Americans already believe: that the system of campaign finance in this country is a legalized form of corruption, and it must end.

Representation. We could revisit a Senate structure that gives the same representation to a state of half a million people as to a state of forty million. The Founders themselves were deeply divided on this question — it was the most contentious battle of the original convention — and they settled it with a compromise born of political necessity, not principle. We are not bound by that necessity any longer. We could reimagine what fair representation looks like in the twenty-first century.

The Electoral College. We could ask whether a system designed in part to accommodate the Three-Fifths Compromise — a system that has, five times now, produced a president who lost the popular vote — still serves the democratic aspirations of this nation.

Executive power. We could confront the extraordinary, bloated power of the modern presidency — a power that no Founder envisioned and that no single human being, regardless of party, should wield. We could establish clear constraints on emergency powers, on war-making, on executive orders that function as legislation by decree.

The judiciary. We could address a Supreme Court that has become the most powerful and least accountable branch of government — lifetime appointments with no enforceable ethical standards, a body of nine unelected individuals whose ideological composition is determined by the accident of mortality and the luck of electoral timing. We could create a system of staggered terms, of expanded membership, of democratic accountability that preserves judicial independence while ending judicial supremacy.

Rights for a new era. We could enshrine the right to vote — explicitly, clearly, and affirmatively, because astonishingly, the Constitution as written does not actually guarantee it. We could address privacy in the digital age. We could establish that every American has a right to clean air and clean water. We could finally write into our foundational charter the full, unequivocal equality of every person regardless of sex, gender, or identity.

This is not radicalism. This is self-governance. This is the very thing the Constitution was designed to make possible.

The Courage Question

Now, I know what the critics will say. They'll say it's too dangerous. They'll say it's too unpredictable. They'll say: "What if the other side takes control?"

And here is my answer: That fear is the disease, not the cure.

We have become so terrified of each other, so convinced that our fellow Americans are the enemy, that we would rather cling to a malfunctioning system than risk the act of collective self-determination. We would rather limp along with a government that serves almost nobody than sit down together and try to build one that serves everybody.

What does that say about us? What does it say about our faith in democracy — in the very idea that free people can govern themselves?

The Founders were not combating fear when they wrote the Constitution. They were swimming in it. They had just fought a war. They represented states with clashing interests, clashing economies, clashing visions. They had every reason to believe the convention would fail. Many of them thought it would fail. They went anyway.

Because they understood something we have forgotten: that the greater danger is always inaction. That a people who lack the courage to reshape their own government will inevitably find that government reshaping them.

An Invitation — Not a Threat

Let me be clear about what I am not saying. I am not saying we should throw the Constitution in the trash. I am not saying the Founders were fools. I am not saying we need to start from a blank page with no respect for what came before.

What I am saying is this: the Constitution is a tool. It is the most extraordinary tool of self-governance ever created. But it is a tool. And when a tool is no longer doing the job, the craftsman doesn't worship the tool — the craftsman improves it.

We improve it not because we hate what came before, but because we love what it was trying to be. We improve it because "a more perfect Union" is not a destination — it is a direction. It is perpetual motion. It is the recognition that every generation must earn its own freedom by adapting the structures of government to the realities of its time.

The men and women who fought for the Bill of Rights, who fought to end slavery, who fought for women's suffrage, who fought for civil rights — every single one of them was told they were going too far, too fast, that the system was fine, that change was dangerous. And every single one of them was right to push forward.

We stand in that tradition tonight.

The Call

So here is my call.

I call on the state legislatures of this nation to exercise their power under Article V. I call on the citizens of this country to demand it of them.

I call on every American who has ever looked at Washington and felt that sinking feeling — the feeling that the game is rigged, that the system doesn't hear you, that your voice doesn't matter — I call on you to recognize that Article V is your voice. It is the one tool in our constitutional order that belongs to the people and the states, that Congress cannot block, that the President cannot veto, that no court can overrule.

It is there because the Founders trusted us. They trusted you. The question is whether we will trust ourselves.

I know the risks. I know the uncertainty. I know that a convention is a leap into the unknown. But I also know this: the status quo is not safe. The status quo is a slow-motion crisis. The status quo is a government that cannot pass a budget, cannot protect voting rights, cannot regulate its own corruption, cannot respond to the existential challenges of our time.

That is the real danger. Not a convention. Not the exercise of self-governance. The real danger is a free people who have grown too frightened to use the freedoms they possess.

Two hundred and thirty-seven years ago, delegates walked into a room in Philadelphia and built a new nation. They were imperfect. Their document was imperfect. But their courage — their courage was extraordinary.

America is asking us for that courage again.

Let us answer.

Let us call the Convention.

Let us, We the People, do what we have always done at our best — not cling to the past, but build the future.

Thank you.

Title: Reclaiming Democracy: The Imperative for a New Constitutional Convention

Introduction
The United States Constitution, drafted in 1787, was hailed as a revolutionary blueprint for self-governance, designed to be “a more perfect union.” Yet, over two centuries later, the system it established has fossilized into a vehicle of dysfunction, inequality, and unrepresentative governance. Despite the Founders’ embrace of adaptability through Article V, the amendment process has become a relic of Gridlock Avenue, where partisanship and entrenched interests paralyze progress. The time has come to invoke Article V’s provision for a constitutional convention—a radical, necessary step to dismantle the systemic flaws crippling our democracy and construct a framework suited to 21st-century challenges.

I. Gridlock and Dysfunction: The Cost of Stagnation
Political gridlock has become the defining feature of American governance. Congress’s approval ratings languish in the single digits, yet legislative productivity has stalled on issues of existential urgency. Climate change, healthcare reform, immigration, and gun safety legislation all languish amid partisan warfare. The filibuster, originally a tool for debate, now functions as a weapon of mass obstruction, requiring a 60-vote supermajority to pass even uncontroversial bills. Meanwhile, government shutdowns—tools of political brinkmanship—cost the economy billions and erode public trust. This dysfunction is not incidental; it is structural. The Constitution’s separation of powers, intended to balance ambition with ambition, instead creates a labyrinth of veto points where progress goes to die. A convention could redesign these mechanisms, replacing dysfunction with streamlined processes that prioritize accountability and legislative efficacy.

II. Undemocratic Institutions: When the Majority Doesn’t Rule
The Constitution’s foundational promise of “we the people” rings hollow in a system where minority rule is Routine. The Senate’s malapportionment grants Wyoming’s 600,000 residents the same representation as California’s 40 million, distorting the will of the majority. The Electoral College, meanwhile, has awarded the presidency four times since 1900—to winners without the popular vote, most recently in 2000 and 2016. These anachronisms undermine the principle of political equality. A constitutional convention could abolish the Electoral College and restructure the Senate, ensuring that every vote—and every voice—counts equally.

III. The Poison of Money in Politics
The Supreme Court’s Citizens United decision in 2010 epitomizes how the current system perpetuates inequality. By equating money with speech, it unleashed a tidal wave of dark money and Super PACs, entrenching the power of the wealthy. Legislators, dependent on corporate donors, cater to the 1% while neglecting the public good. Campaign finance reform languishes because those in power benefit from the status quo. A convention could enshrine public financing of elections and overturn Citizens United, restoring democracy to the people rather than the highest bidder.

IV. A Living Document or a Fossilized Relic?
The Constitution’s rigidity is its Achilles’ heel. Amending it requires a two-thirds majority in Congress and three-fourths of states—a bar so high that only 27 amendments have been ratified in 233 years. Many modern challenges, from digital privacy to AI regulation and climate change, were unimaginable to the Founders. A convention would allow for a holistic update, embedding adaptability and foresight into the document’s core, ensuring it remains a living framework rather than a colonial relic.

V. Judicial Overreach and Underperformance
The Supreme Court, intended as an impartial arbiter, has become a politicized battleground. Lifetime appointments and partisan appointments process have eroded its legitimacy, as seen in the contentious confirmations of Brett Kavanaugh and Amy Coney Barrett. The Court’s composition now hinges on chance and timing, with justices serving for decades, creating generational imbalances. A convention could propose term limits, restructuring, or recusal protocols to restore judicial independence and public confidence.

Addressing Counterarguments
Critics fear a convention might spiral into chaos, with delegates rewriting everything from abortion rights to gun control. Yet, this overlooks the ratification hurdle: any proposal must secure approval from three-fourths of states, a near-impossible threshold for radical extremism. The process itself—rooted in state delegations and democratic deliberation—ensures broad consensus. The greater risk lies in maintaining a system careening toward autocracy, economic collapse, or constitutional crisis.

Conclusion
The United States stands at a crossroads. The Constitution, once a beacon of liberty, now shackles progress in a world of unprecedented complexity. Article V offers a democratic escape clause—a chance to correct the design flaws that enable gridlock, inequality, and unaccountability. A constitutional convention is not a radical act but a return to the Founders’ vision: a government that derives its just powers from the consent of the governed. By embracing this tool, we can forge a more perfect union—one that reflects the diversity, dynamism, and aspirations of the American people in the 21st century. The time for incrementalism is over; the time for renewal is now.

Why a New Constitutional Convention is the Only Solution

The existing mechanisms for reform—legislation and judicial interpretation—are insufficient.
